game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]My playtime:[/b] 10h (based on steam, 100% achievement; 2.5x playthrough)
[b]Grindy Achievement(s):[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement(s):[/b] Yes (17 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement(s):[/b] No.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a massive information gathering system where you, an investigator, is taking a role in sorting the relevant data and fix conflicting data that the system gathered to assist a crime. The game has story branching that persists over 5 chapters.

[b]Pros:[/b]
- 5 chapters
- Multiple endings and story branching that persists over the chapters
- Clean and fresh-looking interface
- You can restart a chapter after you finished the game

[b]Cons:[/b]
- Phone calls and chat animations take a very long time to finish
- Some clues are too hard to deduce unless if you know the full story
- You can't press the button to show conflicting data sometimes

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to read or stalk people, you should buy this game. You also can buy it at a discount if you think that the playtime isn't worth the full price.[/i]

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
The interface is clean and fresh-looking. I like how the summary that is shown at the end of the chapter is introduced; it looks like the workboard in my office except that it's way cleaner.

As someone who likes to try something by doing it firsthand, I don't find the design to be confusing. The portal section looks like your regular website, the message section looks like your regular chat app, and the device section looks like the simpler version of your device.

I'm also impressed by how the dev showed the photos; it looks like a fragmented version of our faces and it looks so detailed even though it's not. The important facial like eyes and hair is shown although most details are blurred and fragmented.

The cutscene at the prologue skipped a few frames to me though, although I don't have any trouble in understanding the story because of that.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The story is being told by several conversations of your "adviser", someone who deduce things based on your findings, and whatever you read when you try to find clues, which are mostly from chat and phone calls.

Even though most conversations are held this way, I didn't find the main story to be confusing. Even if you couldn't understand the story, the "adviser" will give you some sort of info as to what is happening so you should be fine as long as you don't skip it. There's also a summary at the end of the chapter if you want to keep track of things.

There are several branchings in the game, either minor or major. I find the conversation between the branches to be smooth although some parts confused me since I didn't know the whole story at that moment. You need to play several playthroughs throughout the game to get all the major story branches and understand the whole story.

The thing is, there is no good or bad ending in this game; it's all about your opinion. You think what you think is good and bad. You also can deduce the whole story if you want or you can just understand the main story and be done with it.

[h1]The game[/h1]
[b]Features[/b]
There are 3 sections where you do most of your work: portal, message, and device. The in-game name is different, but I can't seem to recall the actual name since you don't need to know about the name to use it.

The portal consists of several web pages that you can access. The pages that you can access are limited to the system and more will show up as you unlock more clues.

The message, on the other hand, is a bit different. A message, either chat, email, or phone, will show up at certain times and you're allowed to wire-tap their chat and calls in real-time. The thing is, the chat speed is very slow. You can speed up the phone chat speed a bit although I still want it to be faster. It's taking too much time to listen to it especially when you're replaying your playthrough.

The device can be activated after you obtain a serial number of the target's device. You can access all files in the device, whether it's from a desktop or phone.

[b]Investigation[/b]
The suspect will have a profile page that you can fill with data. These data can be obtained by browsing through the 3 sections I mentioned. The data that you can take will be highlighted, either in blue or yellow.

Blue-colored means that there is no conflict with the data and yellow means that the data contradicts with other data. The game also has an option to show the conflicting data although I find that it's not working sometimes.

The thing is, you have freedom in choosing whatever you submit. I thought that I should fill all of the highlighted data in blue for complete profiling, but it's actually the opposite. All the data that you fill will be useful for the advisor's judgment and other people's fate, so you should decide carefully on what you submit.

Some data that you submit will change the story greatly, some are not. However, there are times where you have to make a major guess in determining the conflicting data that you must submit because you didn't know much and the clues are too vague at that point. Luckily, as I said before, there are no good and bad endings, so you can proceed as you please.

[b]Replayability and Length[/b]
As I said before, there are multiple endings. There are 5 chapters in total and each chapter except the last one lasts around 1 hour. I played the game fully twice and played one last playthrough from chapter 3 to unlock all of the major branching and achievement. It took me around 4 hours to finish all chapters at once.

Each chapter has a minimum of 2 endings that will affect the subsequent chapter. You can restart the whole story from the beginning or replay the chapter if you want after you finish the game once. Restarting the game from a specific chapter will delete all of the subsequent chapter data though.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
It's a nice game where you have to browse through things and wiretap people's communication to find out whatever is going on. The game has a lot of story branching and replayability.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is fantastic.  It takes the themes expressed in Orwell's 1984 and allows you to take a "big brother" role by reading through social media to decide who is responsible for a series events thought to be done by terrorists.  I was on the edge of my seat the whole time, and it also made me think about every action I took.  Did I want to mark this suspect as potentially dangerous based on an altercation she got into a long time ago?  Is this article an accurate depiction of the person she is now?  Actions like these will come back to haunt you based on the outcomes later in the game.  

Overall, my only complaint with this game is that the ending felt a little too abrupt.  The game is episodic, and the final episode was significantly shorter than every other episode.  Overall, though, I would highly recommend picking this game up.

review_text_raw:
[h1] Spy On Me Daddi Government! [/h1] 
It's probably year 2040, not too far away from present year. Hell projects simillar to Orwell could have been already started, I would not be surprised. Anyways this is a game, that made me forget my troubles for a significant period of time, with it's creative gameplay and story. I usually play for the achievements when the main story is done, and i am often followed by boredom when playing a story for the second time, BUT in Orwell this is not the case. I was very intrigued by how each decision we make impacting the storyline, the ending, it's absolutely marvelous. I love this game! 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2168116860
You play as someone hired by the government and you are investigating a terrorist organization. General gameplay includes reading a lot of useless information and extracting important key data which ultimately the government will make actions. You have access to social media, phones, laptops as long as you piece things together and find ID's, you are in power.  You decide and the daddy government will do the actions. I honestly liked the characters, the insane plot twists of this game. I just hope the devs would make more orwell projects ( yes i know there is another orwell game, but MORE)  You really get into that mind set of a person who would do surveilance and idk it made me a bit uncomfortable but honestly it was fun. Also the art style was bare minimum actually polygonal but you know it fit with the theme, a form of censorship i guess. The music is soo calm and soothing, i also love the random sounds they played when something awful or good happened. This is one of the rarest games where I personally have NOT quit after getting the final achievement, i just wanna know what happens when I save someone or let them go. The game feels like a nice visual novel at times, but makes more sense and proper execution than most good visual novels I have read.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Welcome to Orwellian Big Brother where every action by every citizen of "The Nation" is captured and recorded, and where citizens can be arrested for even the slightest transgression or declaration of anti-Orwell thoughts against The Nation.  You have been recruited by the government as one of its anonymous investigators who must dissect pertinent data and upload this to the government affiliate working with you to prevent a series of terrorist attacks that have been taking place.  Your affiliate can only act on the information you provide (they have no access to the information you have) so your choices matter!

The interface is a joy: very simple and clean, everything very obvious, and the game leads in with a simple tutorial to introduce you to your three tools of Orwell.  On one side of the screen you can open a person's profile to see what information you've gathered on them, and on the other will be their calls messages and mail, with potentially-relevant text highlighted in blue for you to choose whether to add to a person's profile (it cannot be undone if you make a mistake).  You will have to discern who's telling the truth or not, and sometimes you don't have enough information to be 100% sure.  Drag information to a person's profile to attach it to them, and hope you've made the right decision because there is no way to undo this action.

The game would best be described as a combination of simulation, visual novel and point-and-click, but it carries none of the downsides of these games.  Any reading to be done is short, brief and well written, it's really simple to play, and what you can click on is limited to small nuggets of information that the Orwell system deems potentially relevant (and you must decide whether this will help or hinder the government in thwarting the terrorism).  It's not a difficult game, but it's gripping and all too easy to implicate the wrong individual.  At the end I saw the mistakes I'd made.  The best of it is that I somehow suspected that some information was not right as I was playing, but felt compelled to upload it anyway!  My bad!  Replayability is there because there are different outcomes along the way.  The ending is huge but I cannot tell you a thing about it without spoiling the game, but it is worth reaching.

And the soundtrack is amazing.  It's the first time I've ever bought a soundtrack for a game!

If you're unsure, there is a separate playable demo (that's what convinced me to buy the game) and I'm so glad I did.  Yet another great hit for an Indie team who also made the marvellous Hacknet game.  I can't wait to see what Osmotic Studios produce next.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I've had bad experiences with plot-heavy games. Even Telltale's much celebrated titles did very little for me and have contributed to this theory I've had for a long time to video games, in general, seemed incapable of telling a good story. I've always believed that games were much stronger when focusing on mechanics, and those that sacrificed mechanics in favor of plot would always just create an inferior work compared to books or movies.

Orwell is an exception.

What at first might strike you as a fairly preachy "topic of the day" game managed to surpass all my expectations. From the beginning till the end, Orwell and it's characters captivated me.

Orwell is an elegant game. One that understands perfectly how to integrate the agency of it's players to fit into the narrative it's trying to weave, and does so well. Despite the fact that you simply play as a man behind a computer screen, your actions feel like they have consequences, even if sometimes those consequences are ones you don't intend. The longer I played the game, the more I thought about the consequences of every piece of information I submitted, pouring over every bit of data and agonizing over the tiniest nuances of dialogue

While Orwell's themes should be fairly evident from it's title and presentation, I found the plot to be intelligent and far from one-dimensional. Playing the game, often I thought to myself: "Did I make the right call?", "Should I really have told them about that?" I spent a good thirty minutes trying to decide on what I would do during the ending, and even as I write this review I question if I really did the right thing.

To me, that is the hallmark of a good story. One that engages you, makes you feel invested...and above all else; makes you care. It's been a while since I felt so compelled to write a recommendation. But Orwell is one of these games that comes once in a blue moon, and tend to get sadly overlooked. If you couldn't guess already, I highly recommend Orwell. It's one of the best experiences I've had with a story rich game to date, Osmotic Studios has done a fantastic job.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] George Orwell rolls in his grave [/h1]

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is an interactive novel exploring the increasingly popular notion that G. Orwell’s iconic “1984” ended up being a guideline for running a country, rather than a warning to its citizens. True to dystopian tones of its inspiration, the title opens up with a bombing attack on a public plaza. Several people were killed, perpetrators are unknown and public is in an uproar. This where you come in, as hand-picked investigator you will use the latest marvel of civil protection technology – Orwell, to solve the case. Orwell “the first and the last line of defence against terrorism” is a powerful software capable of accessing everything connected to the internet. Once a person is authorised by higher-ups for investigation, you are to upload any useful chunks of data into the software and Orwell will process them, granting you access to further information on the target. Person of interest has their phone number on their social media page? Now you can listen to their calls. An e-mail address published on their company’s website? Let’s take a peek inside. Is that a PC id number? You know the drill by now.

[b] Big brother stays vigilant [/b]
With power of Orwell at your fingertips, the player becomes breach of privacy incarnate, yet the decision whether to upload something or not is yours to make. At times you will have conflicting data, that may mislead the authorities acting upon your investigation, while certain details can be ignored altogether. Orwell is counterintuitive at first and software’s interpretation of data provided is downright puzzling at times. You better adapt to your new role quickly, as at certain junctions your choices will have an impact at the rest of the story.

Your investigation quickly unveils a hint of deeply-rooted conspiracy being at work and bombing is but a beginning of something much bigger. Plot divided into 5 chapters thickens quickly and while the general direction of the story is set in stone, your choices can greatly alter fate of certain characters and the ending is yours to twist.

Orwell is rather straight-forward with its thought-provoking intent. While the title’s plot unveils in delightfully ambiguous “The Nation”, it doesn’t take a particularly big leap of logic to start drawing parallels. Especially with themes of invigilation, media manipulation and a classic question of “whether the ends justify the means”. As with most of such questions and ideas, Orwell will be whatever you choose to make of it. It won’t be long though, as the title takes roughly 5 hours to complete, making it possible to finish Orwell in a single sitting. That said, the story is divided into coherent chapters of similar length, highlighted by the game as a good moment for a break, should you need one. Orwell is commendable for finding multiple sensible ways to underline impending conclusion of a plot thread, while staying reasonable from in-universe perspective.

Another facet of Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You, deserving a separate mention is the art style of the game. Admittedly, the opening cutscene fells remarkably clunky but everything past this very beginning is static images, allowing the style to truly shine. Every picture is built from colourful polygons giving the illustrations believable, yet somewhat obscured, feel to it. Much like the setting of the story, the visuals are deliberately vague, leaving making the parallels up to the player. 

When approached as a book, Orwell makes for enjoyable read with a highly unorthodox mode of delivery. I can easily recommend it to every fan of criminal thriller and political fiction as you should find yourself right at home. If one were to approach the title as a game though, there is very little to speak of. Should you also happen to be the type to skip dialogues in games as a habit, you should probably avoid Orwell like a plague.

[b] DISCLAIMER - As of the time i am writing this review, i only played through one ending. [/b]

Do i recommend Orwell?[b] Absolutely.[/b]

review_text_raw:
Will just jump right into it , given that companies like facebook are throwing our privacy to the wolves(hackers), 3rd party ads etc , this is a perfect time to try out something like orwell to see really how accessing things that are meant to be private can lead to consequences....

If you have played something like papers please then this should be very easy for you to pick up and play , just like it you are a invesitgator recuited to check on a terror attack that took place using the Orwell program. 

At first things seem to be good you are hailed for you work... but how far are you willing to go to nail people to get caught just by selecting their words and thoughts for the moment taken by invading their private life , there are consequences for almost every thing you do.....

I would recommend taking it easy and finishing the game in one go and experiencing the consequences of your actions, without looking up on anything , you can do more playthroughs or go back to chapters to select different paths.
It's an amazing game which will keep asking you the question how far will you let yourself pick on things people say in pirvate . will you do your job as a investigator or follow your ethics ?

Some pros and cons i would like to point out -

Pros 
- Solid game with a proper story and atmosphere to match it.
- Choices there is no game over you play the game and finish in the way you want.
- Covers a lot of real world apps that you can easily connect the dots too.
- Sweet twists in plot will have you clicking around furiously....hehe

Cons
- There is a insanely long load time once you start the game causing many people to think maybe the game is stuck. Also pain if you happened to close the game by mistake will have to sit through the loading again.
- sometimes the hitbox completely misses what you select , this could be a disaster if there is a timed event going on, also for some reason overlay might stop responding (chapter 5)
- Sometimes the indicator which shows whats new to check out might not update casuing you to think that you missed reading something, also sometimes that hints are pretty vaugue leading to some annoying going back to older articles to check if something was missed.
- The ending ....it barely points to anything that there will be a second part or some shocking end game story<after credits> hinting to a second game but if you check the steam store there is a follow up game to this :D .

Overall if you are in the dark as to way some people are extermely worried/against letting their privacy lost that easily check this game out , loved it easily a 8/10.

review_text_raw:
[quote][url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/7871885/]Follow our curator page:[b] OCG-Curations[/b] if you like and want to see more reviews like this one.[/url][/quote]

[h1]Overview:[/h1]
Orwell takes place in a distopian near future in the fictional city of Bonton in The Nation. Orwell is the codename of a vastly advanced surveilance system. They outsource investigations to outsiders of the nation - you! It is your task to spy on suspects and inform the government of what is going on. Basically, you roleplay as "Mr. FBI Man".

[h1]The Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b]Interesting Story[/b] - The game is divided into five chapters, each representing a day in game. I won't be spoiling anything here so there isn't much to say, but I will state my overall impression. The story is good! If you take everything at face value you'll be in for a surprise when you realise this game is not as shallow as it may seem. Each chapter unveils another layer of mystery. There are also three endings (more on that later).

[*][b]Some Replayability[/b] - Every chapter has a few endings (usually two or three). After you finish the game, you may choose to replay starting from any chapter (subsequent ones are erased). Most unique paths you can take are linked to an achievement, so 100%-ing the game is pretty much just exploring every possibility. Don't get too exited though, as that took me about 8 hours and two playthroughs (but in the second one I did consult a guide to save time).

[*][b]Clean UI[/b] - I really like the clean, very intuitive interface. Which is good, considering as this UI is basically the whole game itself. The only downside is that it does not have a dark mode for playing at night, but it's not a dealbreaker.
[/list]

[h1]The Cons:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b]Hand Holding[/b] - You give information to Orwell by drag and dropping data chunks from your spy browser to the Orwell app. They are automatically outlined for you, which seems stupid, but it's a necesarry evil if you think about the programmers. However, one thing I don't like are the special chunks - the conflicts are highlighted in yellow, even if you didn't find both. This makes you extra careful before uploading as one makes the other invalid. This is how the story branches, but if you think about it it's a little stupid. How does the browser know about the conflict if you didn't access the other data chunk yet? This should be up to you - the "detective" to figure out. I wish they were all blue all the time, or turn yellow only after discovering both.

[*][b]Choices Almost Don't Matter[/b] - Remember when I said chapters? Well... they're pretty much isolated instances. Outcomes are mentioned from one to another, but only through slight dialogue changes. But the story progresses the same no matter what you do, until you reach chapter five and finally get to choose an ending.
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
Orwell is a good game because it explores an interesting concept and offers a good story to boot. While it's not as mindbending as I first expected, I still recommended it as a very interactive visual novel. If the topic interests you and don't mind the short playtime, this is a good game to pick up.

review_text_raw:
Orwell is only getting more relevant in the years since it’s release given it’s subject matter of government surveillance. It is kind of a visual novel puzzle game where you navigate different platforms finding bits of info that you can tag to the database which in turn can find you more info. As you go on you start to unravel a story of who was behind the bombings. The bits of info are highlighted so you can’t miss them and you also don’t always have to tag them. This is because some info is out of context. For instance someone saying that they are being tortured by cupcakes is obviously not actual torture but you can still tag the person involved as a torturer. Having the discretion is nice but there are other times where you have to tag certain data to progress that I don’t feel was data that must have been tagged or as relevant as the game made it. I also don’t like how you can’t untag data. I also felt that at the end of the game there was supposed to be multiple ways to handle the outcome but I could only see one or possibly two. I don’t know why the other ways weren’t available to me as I can’t think of a story reason that I shouldn’t have been able to pull off what i wanted. The story was good but the twists near the end were simply fantastic. The UI for the game was easy to get used to and had a good design. I also liked how new parts of the software were revealed as they became needed. The game has no voice acting but that wasn’t an issue wand made sense given the fact that outside of recorded calls this was all  just you at a computer. The puzzle aspect was that you have to scour the various blogs; calls; emails; etc to find info you can use to further the game as well as provide additional depth details and context. 

	I played Orwell on Linux. It froze on me once but other than that I encountered no issues and noticed no spelling errors. There are no graphics options and the game has a 60 FPS cap. You can save on exit but there is just one save slot so you can’t undo choices or have multiple save files. Performance was good with no noticeable lag. Alt-Tab Didn’t work.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
If I could describe [i]Orwell[/i] in just two words, it would be "surprisingly smart". By that I mean: this is, obviously, a game about ubiquitous government surveillance, and that's not exactly a new theme. It would have been really easy to slap a "Big Brother BAD" plot on this, make it all about how you're one lone hero fighting the implacable government machine, give it a nice feel-good ending and be done with it. Or go the other way and go full grimdark with the boot stamping on a human face, forever. But [i]Orwell[/i] avoids taking the easy way out, and presents a very human story about how real people might act in a world where such a surveillance system exists. Sure, all the endings you can get (and there's a few) are still much more optimistic than George Orwell would be comfortable with, but hey, if you want [i]Nineteen Eighty-Four[/i], you know where to get it.

The gameplay is a simple affair where, in your role as a government agent, you look through available information (websites, chat transcripts, telephone calls) and collect relevant "data chunks", which in turn unlock more avenues for gathering information... and that's less boring than I'm making it sound, honest. For starters, it's not completely linear: sometimes the data you can collect is contradictory, irrelevant, or just plain wrong when taken out of context, and you have to apply your best judgement as to what goes in -- and the very fact that you're telling the system what to think of people based on the information you select comes back to haunt you in the story. Still, if you're looking for a puzzle game, or something that will challenge you beyond "did I forget to click on something somewhere", this isn't it. You're basically here for the story, but there's enough agency that you don't feel like you might as well have been reading a novel.

[i]Orwell[/i] isn't perfect. I got "stuck" once or twice when the game wanted me to put in some information I had deemed not worth uploading, or that I'd left to come back to later when I had more data -- the interface will track what you have and haven't seen, but not what you've seen but haven't acted upon. At these points (and some others) suspension of disbelief suffers a bit by the way the game artificially fences off information that, logically, should be available at any time. The graphics, while suitably stylized, are a bit [i]too[/i] stylized, especially when things need to animate. The music is fine (with some dramatic touches for when you've uncovered particularly dramatic info), but not remarkable. None of these things are deal breakers, though, and overall [i]Orwell[/i] is well worth its price tag as a solid, interactive story experience with an "It Could Happen Here!" theme that makes it that much more compelling.

[h1] Final Verdict: Buy [/h1]

Game took me 4 hours to complete 1 playthrough, although you can do multiple playthroughs, depending on what information you find and what connections you make. This game is reading intensive, as you will be sifting through web pages, call logs, chat logs, browser histories, etc. There's also quite a bit of filler information, which is to be expected in this kind of job where you are aggregating huge amounts of data and your job is to sift through that information and find the relevant information.

This game does a great job of putting you in the center of the action as you feel as though you are a real investigator. As the story progresses, you become an even bigger part of the action.

This game isn't for everyone. The gameplay mechanic itself can get tedious at varying times. You really don't stray from what you're doing from the start of Chapter 1 all the way to the conclusion in Chapter 5. So if you don't like parsing information, you will be bored. However, the story keeps it all together and gives purpose to your actions. 

[b]Rate 7/10. Really solid game, interesting story, great ending(s), but the gameplay could have used more variety.[/b]

review_text_raw:
"[i]For how could you establish even the most obvious fact when there existed no record outside your own memory?[/i]"

Anybody who has read through George Orwell's [i]1984[/i] will recognize many prevolent themes throughout this point-and-click adventure. While many movies and games struggle to rival their literary counterparts, Orwell does a spectacular job of demonstrating the themes prevelant in George Orwell's story. While the actual story of the game is different from the book, focusing on the player rather than Winston, many of the aspects are still the same.

I only had a few minor gripes with Orwell that did not take too much away from the story or my immersion. The only real problem that I had with the game was the fact that you had to open each file up to add data to them, rather than just dragging and dropping them onto the character web.

A compelling story with many twists leaves the player hungry for more, available through multiple playthroughs of the game. A second season to Orwell would be very difficult to achieve, due to the ending of the game. I will not go into depth about what this is, as I cannot without spoiling the game.

I strongly reccomend you play through Orwell if you have read the novel [i]1984[/i] or are interested in games with themes of censorship and/or a malleable story.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Conflict:  Orwell is an excellent game that is well designed and well written. 

Conflict: Orwell is a poorly written game that is horribly designed. 

Choose one. 

Orwell is a game that would demand someone choose one of these options, and the problem is is Orwell is an very good game, that is well written.  It however has some horrible design choices that stop me from calling it excellent or perfect.  In fact these design choices are VERY problematic. 


The entire game of Orwell is viewing webpages/conversations/phone calls and hunting down information and uploading it to a major database.  You're allowed free access to almost anything and you can upload almost anything to the database and play with it.  You'll get chastised for uploading garbage information, but it's also kind of fun.  Then the government who hired you to find the information will eventually operate on what you have found.   The story is told through these uploads and the results of your information gathering will change the story.  That's kind of cool. 

And Orwell tells a compelling (if a little predictable) story.  However it ends abruptly and seems to think it's ending can be a lot more impactful than it ends up being.   And then it falls into an egregious hole of pushing replayability but not allowing players to replay part of the story. 

But the thing is Orwell doesn’t really explain it’s gameplay.  The core of the gameplay is not what you upload, but rather what you choose not to upload, or how you choose to resolve conflicts.   But I really hate how it handles conflicts.  What it should do is allow you to upload conflicting information and have you choose how to resolve it explaining more “what do you think?”  Instead it makes this assumption that A or B is right and whichever you choose, they kind of operate on.  However that’s not how the world works, there’s conflicts in a single paragraph and the question is does the guy feel remorseful or does the guy feel responsible for the past… the answer is probably both, why make me choose. 

Then there’s other conflics that seem to not matter.  But what’s really important is what doesn’t get uploaded, and that’s kind of the problem. 

The first game you’re going to upload everything, because that’s what you think is right, but the game is VERY interesting when you don’t upload everything, you can change the game and the story minorly because of this.  You WILL end at the same point, but there is changes that happen. 

Sadly, the ending is a trinary Mass Effect style choice, that feels a bit eyerolling, even the “this ending is only unlocked if X” doesn’t happen and the end is really two or three screens.   I just want more interactivity in the story. 

The other problem is the final episode is actually excellent.  This is the episode where the game shines in a brand new way, it adds a new twist and limits the operator.  I almost wish this twist was added in day two or day three because it makes it much more intense to decide what you do, and I’d have liked to see the decisions on day 2 or 3 affect the ending, perhaps locking off the good ending if you fail. 

You see, the game feels a bit like the Teltale games, low interactivity, always reach the same ending and while that’s true, it’s not the same.  In Telltale, the same things happen no matter what, but in this game, there is changes, I just wish there was bigger meaningful changes that persisted, or even changed the ending and I’m hopeful for the future of Orwell because of that. 

But the story itself is good, if not as interactive as you like.  There’s good story twists, there’s good characters, and I actually like everyone involved in the story.  Orwell is supposed to be about the surveillance state, and even in that way Orwell shines.  And at 5 hours for a full gameplay it might seem expensive, but it can easily be played a second time.  

However replayability does suck, almost the entire game is the same and you have to play at least 3 or 4 hours to replay it.  I wish each episode would be replayable separate so I could go get the three endings of episode 3 and 5 without the full replay.  I didn’t mind a second replay but the third is abusive.

Overall though I DO like Orwell, the litmus test for this game is “did I put season 2 on my wish list” and I did.  I liked it that much.  10 bucks seems high but I think it’s worth the money, and even if not you can get it on sale.  It’s a unique experience, and a fun and interesting take on the surveillance state.  But even my complaint about the design and the way the game really presents it’s gameplay doesn’t ruin and interesting and engaging story. 

I’m hopeful, I want to see season 2 have more interactivity, I want to see season 2 involve more limitations on the user, and I want season 2 to be better, but for a first season of a rather novel game type, I’m pretty happy.  Orwell delivers what it intends to and I do adore how it does so.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The true strength of Orwell lies not in replayability, or even in a strong gameplay mechanic, but in a consuming immersion that relays a story illustrating how powerful a government powered by surveillance could truly be.  You "live" what it would really mean to the lives of people you begin to learn more and about as you coldly monitor them in what feels like real time. 

Unlike other games employing immersive story driven simulations on rails, like "This is the Police" or Uplink, I never once sought to find a "right" solution online.  I accepted that my data was only as good as the research I could see in front of me, and I made some calls based on the psychology of the subjects I digitally (legally) stalked, for the good of The Nation.  By the middle of the game, I couldn't really stop.  It was like binging Netflix, and although pulling back I can clearly see that the game is often holding your hand and guiding you towards the next arc, in the moment the progression feels so natural that I was just excited to unravel the next thread. I performed my role in the Orwell program compliantly. 

The music and the Minority Report style slick UI (that felt so good to work in), combined with the friendly banter of your friendly government advisor led me to the worst part about this game - I started it at 11pm.  I had work at 8am the next day, which only allowed a couple hours of sleep after finally beating the game over 6 straight hours.  

There are unique endings, and the game will bend based on your choices and how far you dig.  When investigating, you don't have to read deeply into every article - Orwell finds the pertinent data for you so you're not forced to muddle through what turns into a mountain of documentation.  Sometimes though, you really need to step back and figure out your suspects murder mystery style, except you do it by going through their files, emails, phone call transcripts, timelines, and chat logs - tying that in with publically available resources. 

And maybe that's the biggest lesson of the game, and of 1984 when you apply a technical layer - in a society where we are constantly generating documents and digital paper trails, you could really learn all you need to know to paint us as however you'd like with the right tools.  It's one thing to read it, but the game lets you feel it. All at once it was exciting, and chilling.

In the end, without offering spoilers, the game never forces you to choose if this is right or wrong.

The total time to beat the game, for me, was 5 hours, but hardly any of that was spent idle. For $10 (I got this on sale at $6), if you have even half the experience I did, the game proves its value quickly.  While you can only replay the game the same way you would reread a book (altered maybe slightly), it did give me a short story worth thinking about for much longer than the gameplay itself lasted.


Pros:

- Immersive gameplay and story
- Great soundtrack
- UI feels fantastic
- Great value
- Story ending felt wrapped up, not abrupt

Cons:

- Limited replayability
- 5 hours of content (I take the time to read a lot of the docs)
- Not super challenging to an average player

[h1] TL;DR "The Last Enemy" without Cucumberpatch [/h1]

Admittedly, the above reference might skate over a few people's heads, but the core themes are the same. Based loosely around the old US Total Information Awareness system, the game explores the issues around predictive profiling and human bias.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A very interesting narrative experience that pulls you in quite well with busywork, much like Papers, Please. It has a very well-crafted and smooth user interface that could totally pass for a real spying program. The game gives you loads of freedom in how you selectively pass on information to alter the plot, and everything from what you choose to save to WHEN you choose to save it can affect the course of the story. At times, these flashpoints are signposted a little too hard, presumably to give players plenty of time to sort through the information at hand and come to a decision, but there are multiple instances when you have to make genunely DIFFICULT choices relying only on your intuition and the information you have gathered thus far. The game does not hold your hand about the consequences your actions will have.

However, the ending did feel a bit contrived and (while foreshadowed well enough), not terribly well justified. I know too well the amount of work that must have gone into such an involved branching story, but the game felt too short. Just when it was beginning to get difficult and the amount of information you had to deal with started to grow burdensome, the game ends. It feels a bit rushed out the door, and doesn't give you enough of a chance to play with the mechanics and start to really sweat. Ultimately, this reveals the underlying issue with Orwell: It is not a game. It is a moral lesson wrapped in an interactive experience. The developers had something they wanted to say, and so the game must come to an end so that they can say it.

I completed the 5-day story in 3-4 hours, but it has some replayability in going back to explore alternate outcomes if you had taken different paths. However, this robs the game of its magic; because you're making difficult decisions based on limited info, a blind playthrough adds a considerable amount. On your second playthrough, you're really just going through the motions to see what happens, which makes the leisurely pace at which characters interact torturous and tends to expose the man behind the curtain when you see how your choices DON'T affect the story.

It has several different endings, which are well-implemented, but the circumstances of the ending's gameplay were so muddled for me that I accidentally clicked my way into an ending I didn't want because I wasn't sure how to do what I wanted to do and I was loaded down with so much unprocessed information I had had to leave for later. The fact that the game jumps at the opportunity to end instead of letting you log out on your own terms when you've done what you want to do doesn't help. This critique probably makes more sense to those who have played it.

All in all, it's a brilliant little dystopia simulator with a lot of love and care poured into it, and a very pleasant and thought-provoking experience I highly recommend. Like any creation, it has its flaws, but it's well worth the price and you can tell how much work went into it.

review_text_raw:
TL;DR: Great for the most part. An intriguing mystery, in-depth characters, very unique gameplay that I heavily enjoyed. Political commentary is heavy-handed but remains interesting, as most characters are morally grey. Great except the ending.

First issue: the late-game twist. I won’t spoil details, but I will talk about the structure of a major late-game twist. I've played this game through 3 times now, and each time the final twist comes out of nowhere. It has foreshadowing in the same way that me saying "you're stupid" foreshadows that I'm going to stab you.
People justify it by making these massive lists of all these barely noticeable details that come together to hint at the idea that "hey, [character] may not be a great person". And then the game jumps from that to terrorism.
Oh, and a lot of the foreshadowing would only come if people made specific decisions. Certain routes would make the twist (which doesn't change) make more or less sense.
The fact that some people think it makes sense and that some people suspected it while playing means that it functionally can't be that bad. To some degree, it makes sense. It did [i]not[/i] land for me though.

Second issue: moral flattening. I noticed something as I progressed through the endings. A bit more spoilery here, but again no specifics. Throughout the game, most characters are morally dubious. Even when you've beaten the game, you'll likely have mixed opinions of a lot of the characters. However, once you reach endings that reveal a bit more information, it becomes clear that there's a real "These people were right the whole time and these people are wrong and kick puppies" mindset. They can't let their actions through the story speak for themselves. There has to be a reveal that the bad guys were doing even worse secret stuff and are unequivocally bad and the good guys are all vindicated.

Get the game though. Two things about the ending miffed me a bit, but I still had a heck of a lot of fun.

review_text_raw:
Personally, I'm loving this game so far. I'll most likely update the review after the next three episodes come out, but I don't believe my opinions will change all that drastically.

Orwell is a game where you investigate a crime (a bombing, to be precise) using the brand-new Orwell system, presumably named after famous author George Orwell, author of 1984. Using the program, you can identify data that might be necessary to your investigation, slowly collecting it and linking it together to form a case for your superior to take a look at and give his verdict.

Some data is useless; do you really need to know what this woman's favourite colour or food is? Is someone's address being "somewhere over the rainbow" on one of their social networking profiles pertinent information to the case? No, and adding too much useless data can cloud the system, leading to the wrong conclusion by your supervisor at the end. One of my personal favourites was having someone logged in on someone else's account mention their profession, and it came up as data for the account's owner. Presumably, if in an online chat, you joked you killed a man, or were a descendant of King Arthur, that would show up in the Orwell system as important information.

Other data is in conflict; for example, if a Facebook timeline would have someone changing their relationship status to "in  a relationship with whoever", and then later changing it to "single", which one would be the correct data to input? You cannot remove data once you upload, so you have to think long and hard about which to use. Of course, in this example, you could look at whichever was more recent, but the decisions can be harder and more complicated than that, I promise you. I commend this game having pieces of in-conflict data show up as conflicted even if you haven't found the other data yet, so you can't choose A (the only option at the time) and then have option B, the secret correct answer, be revealed to you later.

You also have the ability to, once you have contact details (such as phone numbers, email addresses, etc.), access your target's phone calls, emails, chat histories. These play out in real time, but you can easily go back to searching through websites for info, and return once the conversation is done.

And I won't spoil anything, but the ending of the second episode had me almost falling off my seat in anticipation and anxiety, hoping my guesses weren't wrong. I punched the air and shouted "YES" pretty loudly when it was revealed I was correct. The game got me way more emotionally involved than I was expecting.

If the idea of this interests you, buy the game. It'll definitely be worth the money. If you're on the fence, never fear! There is a free demo which contains the first episode of five. You now have no reason not to go try it. Go try it.

While there are a couple choices that cement the final ending, the majority of the game is spelled out for you, but that's okay, this is an amazing story and worth the hand-holding.

There are a few choices that will change the story significantly, and these choices will create different endings, allowing you to play through the story a few times as different investigators before the game truly "ends" so you can get the whole story. The only con, a large one in my opinion, is that the game babies you and holds your hand. All answers are highlighted to you. Large red (!) signs appear when there is a pertinent piece of information in that story. NON-STORY SPOILER: [spoiler]At the later end of the game, you are limited on how much information you can process, meaning there is literally no skill or real cognitive function required to do your detective work.[/spoiler] For a game that has the feeling of a detective thriller, you are practically on rails to what is already being laid out for you. Overall, this is a masterpiece of a novel, it emulates the fearmongering that comes from modern technologies, and has the potential to give you goosebumps from the twists and turns you, the lone investigator finds on the trail. While there are a couple choices that cement the final ending, the majority of the game is spelled out for you, but that's okay, this is an amazing story and worth the hand-holding.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell takes sort of a visual novel framework and bends it until it looks something like a mass surveillance simulator. You're a foreign contractor working within a series of ethical safeguards to perform ethical mass surveillance (if such a thing is possible) for another country's government. And it's an interesting time to be an Orwell contractor, because The Nation is in the grips of a terrorist bombing spree. Your actions and possibly even inaction can bend the arc of the story.

Like most visual novels, your actions don't have major impacts on larger direction of the plot, but they change the details along the way and might make you more sympathetic to ending the game in one way or another. It's neat to go back and see how changes affect things and unlock other achievements, but it does get a little tedious since waiting through real-time chat and phone conversations is a lot less exciting the second time around.

Overall, I had a pretty good time, but most people will probably be one-and-done and put up fewer hours accordingly. Weigh that against how much you're willing to spend.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
You play through this game incredibly fast, but as someone who's a massive fan of everything dystopian, this is an absolutely brilliant concept! You get to decide on what will happen to people based on your own first impressions and what the media writes about them. You have to judge based on intuition and you'll notice at one point or another that you might judge too quickly because certain people might be in your allergy-space or because they might've written a regrettable facebook message. 
I really really hope that the developers will put out more stories with this concept (even though there is a bit of a closed ending) because I absolutely loved the gameplay of it and the decision making involved with it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
First Playthrough: 

A short neat game experience with an interesting dystopian espionage theme. Simple and straight forward game mechanics kept my engagement high throughout the entire first run through of the game. Overall story was enthralling given the intrigue and mystery surrounding a web of individually well written characters that share a common "Thought". The usage of dramatic and impactful audio queues during moments of revelation help to sell the importance of key information to the story and make them memorable. 

Some negatives I find with this game is that in portions I tend to find myself feeling lost with what I should be looking for but the game does provide help icon hints to direct your attention to where you need to me, just sometimes those hints are not provided for every situation. Personally I find the ending to be a little too narrowing forcing you to choose between three separate paths and any of which leaves questions of the overall story unresolved unless you replay through the game till the end. This does encourage replayablity of at least three different experiences of the game, and with several side choices throughout, but still leaves a feeling, that after my first playthrough, doesn't leave me feeling completely satisfied.

Overall, for what the game is gunning to be, I'll give the experience an 8/10 despite my issues with the final act of the game.
